title: Refresh-Ahead Pattern
description: Learn refresh-ahead caching, where a background worker proactively refreshes Redis keys before they expire to prevent latency spikes.

data.text: Refresh-ahead is a proactive caching strategy. Instead of waiting for a cache miss to repopulate data, a background process refreshes keys before their TTL expires. This eliminates the latency spike that occurs when a popular key is missing and must be loaded from the database.

Each cached key is stored with a TTL. The application also records an expected refresh time slightly before expiration, often by using a sorted set where the score is the refresh deadline. A background worker polls for keys that are approaching their refresh window, loads fresh data from the database, and updates Redis before users request the stale data.

data.title: Refresh flow:
items: On write, store data in Redis with a TTL and register the refresh deadline in a sorted set.
A background worker queries the sorted set for keys whose refresh deadline is near.
The worker loads the latest data from the database.
The worker updates Redis and resets the TTL.
The worker updates the refresh deadline in the sorted set.

data.text: In cache-aside or read-through, the first request after a key expires pays the full database latency. For high-traffic endpoints, that single slow request can cascade into connection pool exhaustion or thread saturation. Refresh-ahead removes that penalty by ensuring the cache is always warm for hot data.

data.caption: Refresh-ahead background worker
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Worker
    participant Redis
    participant DB
    loop Every 30 seconds
        Worker->>Redis: ZRANGEBYSCORE refresh:products -inf <now+60s>
        Redis-->>Worker: [product:10, product:42]
        Worker->>DB: SELECT * FROM Products WHERE Id IN (10,42)
        DB-->>Worker: product rows
        Worker->>Redis: SET product:10 <fresh> EX 600
        Worker->>Redis: ZADD refresh:products <new-deadline> product:10

Refresh Window
data.text: Refresh-ahead works best when the refresh window is short enough that keys rarely become stale, but long enough to avoid unnecessary database load. A common starting point is to refresh when 10-20 percent of the TTL remains.

terms.definition: The period before key expiration during which the background worker starts refreshing the key.
A sudden increase in response time caused by cache misses that force requests to wait for the database.

items.question: Does refresh-ahead replace TTLs?
items.answer: No. TTLs are still needed as a safety net. The background worker keeps hot keys warm, but the TTL ensures that unpopular keys are eventually evicted.

items.question: What if the worker fails to refresh in time?
items.answer: The application should still handle cache misses gracefully as a fallback. Refresh-ahead reduces misses; it does not eliminate the need for a fallback read path.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Refresh-ahead removes latency spikes by warming the cache proactively.
A background worker uses a sorted set to track refresh deadlines.
Hot keys are refreshed before they expire; cold keys still fall back to the database.
Pair with TTLs and cache-miss fallbacks for resilience.
data.takeaway: Refresh-ahead is ideal for high-traffic read-heavy workloads where consistent low latency matters.

data.title: Add Refresh-Ahead to a Leaderboard
data.description: A game leaderboard is read thousands of times per minute. A cold key means a slow response.
steps: Cache the top-100 leaderboard in Redis with a 5-minute TTL.
Store the leaderboard refresh deadline in a sorted set.
Build a background worker that refreshes the leaderboard when 1 minute remains.
Simulate 1,000 concurrent leaderboard requests while the worker refreshes.
Verify that response times stay low and no cache misses occur.
data.expectedOutcome: The leaderboard is always warm, and concurrent requests never see a cold cache.
